content: Hypertonic saline is known to enhance mucociliary clearance and may reduce the inflammatory damage in the airways of individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of nebulised hypertonic saline compared to placebo or other treatments that promote mucociliary clearance. The review included 24 trials with a total of 1,318 participants ranging in age from one month to 56 years. However, 15 of these trials were judged to have a high risk of bias due to participants being able to distinguish the taste of the solutions. Additionally, 29 trials were excluded, two are ongoing, and six are awaiting classification. Hypertonic saline (3% to 7%) versus placebo in stable disease: The evidence is very uncertain regarding whether regular use of nebulised hypertonic saline improves lung function, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) % predicted, after four weeks of treatment (mean difference [MD] 3.30%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.71 to 5.89; 4 trials, 246 participants; very low-certainty evidence). In preschool children, no difference in lung clearance index (LCI) was observed at four weeks. However, a small improvement in LCI was noted after 48 weeks of treatment with hypertonic saline compared to isotonic saline (MD -0.60, 95% CI -1.00 to -0.19; 2 trials, 192 participants). There is uncertainty about whether hypertonic saline affects mucociliary clearance, pulmonary exacerbations, or adverse events compared to placebo. Hypertonic saline versus control during acute exacerbations: Two trials compared hypertonic saline to control, but only one provided data. There may be little or no difference in lung function (FEV1% predicted) after treatment with hypertonic saline compared to isotonic saline (MD 5.10%, 95% CI -14.67 to 24.87; 1 trial, 130 participants). Neither trial reported deaths or measures of sputum clearance. No serious adverse events were observed. Hypertonic saline versus recombinant deoxyribonuclease (rhDNase): Three trials compared hypertonic saline to rhDNase, with two trials (61 participants) providing data. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of hypertonic saline on FEV1% predicted after three weeks (MD 1.60%, 95% CI -7.96 to 11.16; 1 trial, 14 participants; very low-certainty evidence). At three months, rhDNase may lead to a greater improvement in FEV1% predicted compared to hypertonic saline in participants with moderate to severe lung disease (MD 8.00%, 95% CI 2.00 to 14.00; low-certainty evidence). There is uncertainty about differences in adverse events between the two treatments. No deaths were reported. Hypertonic saline versus amiloride: One trial (12 participants) compared hypertonic saline to amiloride but did not report most of the outcomes of interest. The trial found no difference between the treatments in measures of sputum clearance (very low-certainty evidence). Hypertonic saline versus sodium-2-mercaptoethane sulphonate (Mistabron®): One trial (29 participants) compared hypertonic saline to sodium-2-mercaptoethane sulphonate. The trial did not measure primary outcomes. No differences were observed between treatments in measures of sputum clearance, antibiotic courses, or adverse events (very low-certainty evidence). Hypertonic saline versus mannitol: One trial (12 participants) compared hypertonic saline to mannitol but did not report lung function outcomes at relevant time points. No differences in sputum clearance were observed, but mannitol was reported to be more irritating (very low-certainty evidence). Hypertonic saline versus xylitol: Two trials compared hypertonic saline to xylitol. The evidence is very uncertain regarding differences in FEV1% predicted or median time to exacerbation between the two groups (very low-certainty evidence). No other outcomes were reported. Hypertonic saline 7% versus hypertonic saline 3%: The evidence is very uncertain regarding whether 7% hypertonic saline provides greater improvement in FEV1% predicted compared to 3% hypertonic saline (very low-certainty evidence). Conclusions: The evidence is very uncertain about whether regular use of nebulised hypertonic saline improves lung function in adults and children over 12 years of age with CF after four weeks of treatment (three trials; very low-certainty evidence). No difference was observed at 48 weeks (one trial; low-certainty evidence). In children under six years of age, hypertonic saline modestly improved LCI. Evidence from one small trial suggests that rhDNase may lead to better lung function than hypertonic saline at three months, but no differences were observed in secondary outcomes. Hypertonic saline appears to be a useful adjunct to physiotherapy during acute exacerbations of lung disease in adults. Overall, the certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to low. Future research should focus on the role of hypertonic saline in conjunction with cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy.
